metadata.file_name: 42. Gil-Madrona et al. (2025). What Are the Best Predictors of STEM Competences in PISA 2018? An Analysis of the Spanish Context Using Data Mining.pdf
metadata.title: What Are the Best Predictors of STEM Competences in PISA 2018? An Analysis of the Spanish Context Using Data Mining

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses PISA 2018 microdata for Spain obtained from the Spanish INEE public database. The analytic sample is restricted to students with complete data for all variables of interest and for the mathematics and science criterion competences, yielding 35,943 students aged 15 years. The manuscript does not report applying PISA complex survey weights (e.g., student/sampling weights) or replicate-weight procedures; therefore, it is unclear whether estimates account for the two-stage clustered sampling design. For the data-mining stage, the authors perform extensive predictor recategorization and elimination of low-information variables (imbalanced categories, variables with ≥70% empty records) and then run 10-fold cross-validation; however, the weighting strategy for the predictive models is not documented.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: The dependent variables are PISA mathematics and science competences, which in PISA are typically derived from plausible values (PVs). However, the paper does not describe whether PVs were used directly, averaged, or combined using Rubin’s rules, nor does it specify any PV-related software workflow. This is a reporting gap because PV handling is central to valid uncertainty estimation for PISA achievement outcomes.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Used Spanish students participating in PISA 2018. Restricted to students aged 15 years (15.25–16.17) and in the 4th year of Secondary Education (ISCED 3, 10th grade) who had been in the educational system for at least 6 years. Further restricted to cases with complete data for all variables of interest and for achievement in mathematical and scientific competences (complete-data criterion). During preprocessing, predictors were recategorized to balance categories; variables with only two categories where >85% of responses fell in one category were eliminated; and variables with ≥70% empty records were eliminated. Highly correlated predictors were removed using Cramer's V, and the remaining predictors were organized into sets of 20–100 variables for model runs.

main_findings.performance_metrics: R² (reported as prediction percentage) via 10-fold cross-validation: Ridge 56.10% (±0.01%), SVR 55.92% (±0.01%), Random Forest 54.84% (±0.02%) when 100 variables were introduced.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2018 Grade 10 Mathematics data for Spanish students, the study leveraged ICT availability and use, well-being, supportive school context, household possessions/home indices, and metacognition to predict mathematical competence achievement, finding that the Ridge model achieved the highest prediction percentage (56.10%) among the three data-mining methods. This indicates that strengthening ICT-related learning opportunities alongside student well-being and supportive school conditions may be a high-leverage strategy for improving mathematics performance, though the study is cross-sectional and does not establish causal effects.

main_findings.performance_metrics: R² (reported as prediction percentage) via 10-fold cross-validation: Ridge 62.27% (±0.02%), SVR 62.12% (±0.01%), Random Forest 55.22% (±0.01%) when 100 variables were introduced.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2018 Grade 10 Science data for Spanish students, the study leveraged well-being, supportive school context, metacognition, mother tongue/reading-related variables, and economic/cultural parent level to predict scientific competence achievement, finding that the Ridge model achieved the highest prediction percentage (62.27%) among the three data-mining methods. This indicates that science improvement efforts should pair emotional and contextual supports with metacognitive strategy development and reading/language supports, while recognizing that the analysis cannot infer causality from predictive associations.

data.outcome_summary: This study performs a secondary analysis of PISA 2018 microdata for Spain, focusing on students aged 15 (analytic sample: 35,943) and predicting two STEM competences: mathematics and science. After extensive preprocessing (recategorization, removal of highly imbalanced/near-empty predictors, correlation screening, and averaging of 10 PISA-derived target variables per competence), the authors train three data-mining models—Random Forest, support vector regression (SVR), and ridge regression—using 10-fold cross-validation. With 100 introduced predictors, prediction performance (reported as R²/prediction percentage) was highest for ridge: 56.10% (±0.01%) in mathematics and 62.27% (±0.02%) in science. The most influential predictor domains differ by competence: ICT-related variables dominate mathematics, while science emphasizes well-being/supportive context, metacognition, and mother tongue/reading. Limitations include cross-sectional design (no causal inference) and incomplete transparency on plausible-value handling for PISA achievement outcomes.
